a b s t r a c t
In this study, the effect of Cl activation treatment on performance indicators of CdS/CdTe solar cells was
investigated. We improved the performance of CdTe solar cells by applying a novel double treatment
method that combines the CdCl2 dipping treatment and Freon (difluoro chloromethane) treatment
methods that were previously studied. Conventional CdCl2 methanol dipping treatment (CdCl2 dipping
treatment), Freon gas treatment that includes chlorine (Freon treatment), and CdCl2 dipping treatment
+ Freon treatment (double treatment) were performed, and the efficiencies, open circuit voltage (VOC),
and short circuit current (JSC) for all three processes were observed. Although the efficiencies of the
CdCl2 dipping treatment and Freon treatment were similar, there was a trade-off between the VOC and
JSC in both processes. The double treatment sample shows an efficiency of 14.3%, which was higher
than that of a single-treated sample. To investigate the characteristic change of each part of the solar
cell, an equivalent circuit model in which the device was divided into a main junction and a back
contact was used. In addition to electrical measurements, secondary ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS)
and time of flight (TOF) analysis were performed. Through TOF measurement, drift mobility values for
three treatment samples were calculated to be 1.1 cm2/Vs, 1.8 cm2/Vs, and 1.9 cm2/Vs, respectively.
With TOF measurement, it was proved that the double treatment had a significant influence on the
efficiency of the sample.

wide. Recently, CdTe solar cell technology has achieved a de-
vice efficiency close to 22% (Green et al., 2019). Today, it is
the most promising thin-film technology with a high market
share. Although 22% efficiency has been reported, the achiev-
able value for CdTe is 33%, according to the Shockley–Queisser
limit for single-junction solar cells (Shockley and Queisser, 1961;
Polman et al., 2016). Therefore, to reach that efficiency level, fur-
ther research on the interface, junction, and electrical contact of
CdTe-based solar cells is necessary. Unlike other thin-film devices

et al., 2012), CdTe achieves high conversion efficiency through
the Cl activation process. High-temperature post-treatment in
a chlorine-containing atmosphere is performed regularly to in-
crease the grain size and improve layer quality. Since the Cl

2. Experiments & measurements
2.1. Sample fabrication
Here, the device with the superstrate structure was configured
by depositing Corning 7059 glass having a 100 nm thick indium
tin oxide (ITO) layer. On this layer, CdS films having a thickness
of 100 to 150 nm were deposited by PVD using a high purity CdS
powder (99.995%, Sigma Aldrich) at a substrate temperature of
200 ◦C and deposition rate of 3 Å/s. Subsequently, a CdTe layer
having a thickness of 5–6 µm was sequentially deposited by PVD
at a substrate temperature of 350 ◦C. Activation treatment of the
CdTe cells was carried out in two ways: CdCl2 dipping treatment
and Freon treatment. In the CdCl2 dipping treatment, the cells
were dipped in a supersaturated CdCl2 methanol solution and
annealed in a furnace at 350–450 ◦C. In the Freon treatment,
a mixture of CHF2Cl and Ar gases was used. The pressure of
CHF2Cl was 40 mbar, and the total pressure of Ar and CHF2Cl was
400 mbar. Under such controlled pressure, the CdTe cells were
annealed at 400–450 ◦C for <30 min. Typically, Freon dissociates
approximately above 400 ◦C to produce chlorine, which subse-
quently reacts with CdTe to form CdCl2. The process aids in the
recrystallization and passivation of grain boundaries.
In this study, the double treatment of the sample was carried
out by performing CdCl2 dipping treatment, followed by the Freon
treatment. The Freon treatment was carried out at a temperature
above 430 ◦C. In addition, a sample without chlorine activation
was fabricated as a reference. Before the deposition of the back-
contact, the CdTe surfaces were etched with an NP solution to
remove the CdCl2 residue and form a heavily doped p + layer. Cu
(4 nm) and Au (100 nm) were deposited by magnetron sputtering
to form the back-contact. Finally, the samples were annealed at
190 ◦C for <20 min for activating the back-contact region.
2.2. Equivalent circuit modeling
For analyzing the structural configuration of the device, we
constructed an equivalent circuit of the main junction region and
back-contact interface. The entire stack structure of the device
(i.e. Au/CdTe/CdS/TCO) (Fig. 1) consists of two diode regions.
These are the diodes in the back-contact area of CdTe/Au and the
p–n junction diode of CdTe/CdS. By analyzing the characteristics
of both the diode regions, we can estimate the contribution of
each region to the performance variation of the device. There-
fore, we conducted experiments for quantitative analysis of the
device performance improvement by analyzing each part of the
equivalent circuit. CdTe acts as a p-type semiconductor with a
large electron affinity and bandgap of approximately 4.5 and 1.5
eV, respectively. The back-contact metal layer and the CdTe layer
form a Schottky barrier, which is depicted as two back-to-back
diodes in the equivalent circuit model.

The performance of the CdTe cells was evaluated using
current–voltage (J–V) characteristic analysis under AM 1.5 illumi-
nation with a power density of 100 mW/cm2. The key parameters
of the solar cell were average values of 5 sample datapoints for
each treatment method. The error value was specified to be the
standard deviation. Table 1 lists the main parameters of the solar
cell along with error values in each parameter.

4. Conclusion
The change in some of the sample characteristics (such as
JSC and VOC) according to the activation of the CdTe layer in
CdCl2 dipping treatment, Freon treatment, and double treatment
was analyzed. Using an equivalent circuit model, the device was
divided into main junction and back-contact to identify changes
in efficiency and characteristics. Since there is approximately
no change in barrier height in the back-contact region due to
the treatment methods, the change in efficiency results from
the changes in the main p–n junction caused by the treatment
processes. The change in JSC for each treatment method shows
the dependence on drift mobility derived by the TOF method. The
single treatment represents a trade-off relationship depending on
the method. For Voc, a value of 0.78 V was achieved in CdCl2 dip-
ping treatment and a value of 0.70 V for Freon treatment. For Jsc,
a value of 23.6 mA/cm2 was achieved in CdCl2 dipping treatment
